voice_over.title: The Breaking Point of Database Contention
voice_over.narration: Now that our report queries are tuned, we need to look at a deeper problem: contention, where reports and live traffic fight over the same database. Let's look at why shared databases eventually reach a breaking point. In G M S today, every service shares a single sequel database. That works well while reporting is light. But picture gym owners running large end-of-month reports. These reports run heavy aggregations that scan many thousands of rows. When those queries hit the same database that handles live member signups, they compete for the same processor, memory, and disk, and can starve the everyday write path. The result is that live operations, like processing payments, can slow to a crawl because the database is too busy calculating totals. This resource starvation is a classic performance bottleneck. In Rationale for a Dedicated Reports Service, we split reporting into its own service but kept one shared database. Separating the database work as well is the natural next step when load grows, because protecting the primary database from query spikes is critical for uptime. The key idea is that shared infrastructure limits our ability to scale processing power independently.

voice_over.title: Isolation via a Read Replica
voice_over.narration: Since we understand why shared database resources cause bottlenecks, let's explore how a specialized copy of the database can isolate heavy traffic. A common industry fix is a read replica, a read-only copy of the database that takes heavy analytical reads away from operational traffic. G M S does not run one today. Think of the primary database as a busy cashier handling new signups, while the replica is a photocopy of the ledger handed to an accountant. The accountant does their work without ever bothering the cashier. This strategy relies on isolation. If the reports service pointed at the replica, a massive report with large joins would only use the replica's resources. Giving the reports service its own connection pool, a pre-warmed set of reusable database connections, keeps its load contained too. The key idea is isolated workloads. In short, replicas protect operational traffic from heavy analysis.

voice_over.title: Managing Hanging Queries and Blast Radius
voice_over.narration: Building on the query optimizations we previously explored, let's see what happens when those analytical queries get stuck. On a single shared database, a hung report keeps holding processor and memory that live requests need, and slows everyone down. A replica contains the blast radius, which is the maximum collateral damage a slow or hanging query can cause to surrounding services. If a report hangs on the replica, the primary database is untouched and signups carry on. With the reports service in its own silo, stuck queries become easier to manage. You can set strict timeouts or restart the replica entirely without affecting the primary system. G M S sets no database query timeouts today, so this is part of the same future option. The key idea is contained failure. Simply put, report issues would no longer threaten core operations.

voice_over.title: The Reality of Replication Lag
voice_over.narration: While isolation provides great stability, it introduces a necessary trade-off in how we view our data. The catch is replication lag, which is the brief delay between when data is written to the primary database and when that change copies over to the replica. Because this copying process is asynchronous, the replica can briefly lag behind the primary. This results in eventual consistency, a data model where copies are guaranteed to match the source eventually, but might return seconds-old data. For analytical reports, being a few seconds behind is an acceptable trade-off for speed and stability. However, you would never use a replica for security-sensitive checks where perfect accuracy is needed immediately. Teams that run replicas monitor this lag closely to keep it within healthy limits. The key idea is eventual consistency. The main takeaway is that data on a replica might be slightly stale.

voice_over.title: Architectural Health and Fallback
voice_over.narration: Finally, let's consider what happens when a replica setup needs maintenance or encounters a failure. A healthy replica setup uses lag as its main warning sign. If the replica struggles or fails, the fallback is to point the reports service back at the primary database for a while. That is less efficient, but it keeps reports online while the replica is fixed, and business data stays accessible. Moving reporting traffic to a replica turns a growing performance bottleneck into an isolated, scalable workload. The key idea is architectural resilience: replicas isolate and scale data-heavy analytical needs. G M S keeps one database for now, and this is the path it can take as data volumes grow. Next, we will look at work that should not run inside a request at all.
